Having said this, as he was making efforts to flee with his followers,

children.text: sa susrāva bhayānmūtraṃ tāvadetya bhaṭairvṛtaḥ // KNarm_3.94 //
children.translated_text: he urinated out of fear, and just then was surrounded by arriving soldiers. // 3.94 //

children.text: sa rājñā hṛtasarvasvaḥ praklinno bandhane ciram /
children.translated_text: Stripped of all possessions by the king, soaked and in prison for a long time,

children.text: dhanena veśyayā svasrā mocito niragāttataḥ // KNarm_3.95 //
children.translated_text: he was freed through the wealth of a courtesan—his sister—and then came out. // 3.95 //
Then, bereft of wealth, he became a mutterer of prayers, an interpreter of dreams,
bowing to everyone, flattering, and speaking sweetly. // 3.96 //
The official who once stood erect and stiff like a <s>liṅga</s>,
upon losing his office, became like an old man's scrotum. // 3.97 //
For those blinded by the intoxication of power, always with angry glances,
imprisonment is the supreme eye-salve that produces clarity of vision. // 3.98 //
He who despises even the venerable when they fall at his feet in distress,
when fallen from power, bows down to feet smeared with excrement. // 3.99 //

children.text: aho bata muhūrtena bhavanti na bhavanti ca /
children.translated_text: Alas! In a moment they exist and then exist no more—
the fortunes of officials are as fleeting as the flames of burning straw. // 3.100 //
When his wife got up and left of her own accord, he, now destitute,
wandered about, a repository of wretchedness, seeking food at the homes of relatives. // 3.101 //
Rough, emaciated, extremely filthy, wearing stitched and burnt rags,

children.text: piśāca iva duṣprekṣyo dinaireva babhūva saḥ // KNarm_3.102 //
children.translated_text: he became horrible to look at like a <s>piśāca</s> (demon) within just days. // 3.102 //
With buttocks, scrotum, and belly burned by the heat of a chaff-fire brazier,
with a cord tied around his knees to ward off wind-colic, // 3.103 //
with throat and stomach seized from swallowing the wealth of gods and Brahmins,
with a belly shrunken from hunger, mouth parched, fallen, wandering in filth, // 3.104 //
with knees and feet gnawed by dogs, streaming much blood,
contented with balls of food given out of pity, eating leftovers, // 3.105 //
with his hairy testicles protruding from half-burnt rags,
with head, shoulders, chest, and sides smeared with ash, shameless, // 3.106 //
babbling, longing for a small coin, given some gruel by someone,
rejected from drinking at the water-station by the keeper who mistook him for a <s>Ḍomba</s> (outcaste). // 3.107 //
With his body covered by a menstruating woman's straw in winter,
in a quarrel with beggar children over broken pot-shards,
his eyebrows, beard, and eyes burned by a blow from a fire-vessel, // 3.108 //
beaten repeatedly with clubs by <s>Caṇḍālas</s> at funerals,
lying in mud, he cried out on the roads leading to charity-houses and holy places. // 3.109 //
Then, having fallen face-down in the royal excrement drain,
with his hips raised high, that worst of men gave up his life. // 3.110 //
Thus, through the austerity of destitution, he was reduced to nothing but bones,

children.text: saśarīraḥ svayaṃ prāpto narakaṃ narakaṇṭakaḥ // KNarm_3.111 //
children.translated_text: and that thorn among men reached hell in his own body. // 3.111 //
Thus, when the official-courtier fires gradually subsided,
the people, freed from affliction, rejoice, blessed with contentment. // 3.112 //
Thus this <s>Narmamālā</s> (Garland of Jests) has been composed, a discussion of the wicked conduct and evil deeds of the assemblies of official-courtiers;

children.text: api sujanavinodāyombhitā hāsyasiddhyai kathayati phalabhūtaṃ sarvalokopadeśam // KNarm_3.113 //
children.translated_text: though fashioned for the amusement of good people and the achievement of humor, it tells a teaching for all people as its fruit. // 3.113 //

body.translated_text: Thus ends the third jest in the <s>Narmamālā</s>.
Thus concludes the <s>Narmamālā</s>.
This is the work of <s>Kṣemendra</s>, also known as <s>Vyāsadāsa</s>. May there be auspiciousness.
